title: Elementary Reactor Physics
short_intro: Elementary reactor physics deals with the neutron chain reaction, moderation, and the steady-state conditions necessary for controlled nuclear fission energy generation. It utilizes neutron transport and diffusion parameters to determine critical sizes of nuclear reactors.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic concepts of nuclear fission, chain reactions, role of moderators (graphite, heavy water), control rods, and prompt versus delayed neutrons.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Multi-group diffusion theory, neutron life cycle (four-factor formula), effective multiplication factor, Fermi age theory, and reactor kinetics.

prerequisites: Binding energy per nucleon curve and mass defect
Nuclear cross-section and mean free path

concept_notes.heading: Nuclear Fission and Neutron Production
bullets: Absorption of a thermal neutron by a fissile nucleus such as <sup>235</sup>U produces an excited compound nucleus <sup>236</sup>U<sup>*</sup> which undergoes asymmetric fission.
Fission releases an average of ~2.4 to 2.5 fast neutrons per absorption event alongside fission fragments and ~200 MeV of energy.
Most neutrons released are prompt (emitted within 10<sup>-14</sup> s), while a small fraction (~0.65% for <sup>235</sup>U) are delayed neutrons emitted by fission product decay.

concept_notes.heading: The Four-Factor Formula (Fermi's Theory)
bullets: The infinite multiplication factor (k<sub>inf</sub>) is the ratio of thermal neutrons produced in generation (n+1) to thermal neutrons in generation (n) in an infinite medium.
It is expressed as k<sub>inf</sub> = ε p f η, where ε is the fast fission factor, p is the resonance escape probability, f is the thermal utilization factor, and η is the reproduction factor.

For a finite reactor, leakage must be accounted for, yielding the effective multiplication factor k<sub>eff</sub> = k<sub>inf</sub> L<sub>f</sub> L_t, where L_f and L_t are non-leakage probabilities for fast and thermal neutrons respectively.

concept_notes.heading: Neutron Moderation and Thermalization
bullets: Fast neutrons lose kinetic energy predominantly through elastic scattering collisions with light moderator nuclei like hydrogen, deuterium, or carbon.
Good moderators possess a high scattering cross-section (σ<sub>s</sub>), a low absorption cross-section (σ<sub>a</sub>), and a large average logarithmic energy decrement per collision (ξ).
Thermal neutrons reach thermal equilibrium with the moderator atoms at ambient temperature, possessing a most probable energy of ~0.025 eV.

concept_notes.heading: Reactor Control and Kinetics
bullets: Reactor operation is governed by the effective multiplication factor: k<sub>eff</sub> = 1 (critical, steady state), k<sub>eff</sub> > 1 (supercritical, power rising), and k<sub>eff</sub> < 1 (subcritical, power falling).
Control rods composed of strong neutron absorbers like boron, cadmium, or hafnium are inserted or withdrawn to adjust the thermal utilization factor (f) and maintain criticality.
Delayed neutrons play a vital role in reactor safety by extending the effective neutron generation time, making manual and automatic control feasible.

derivations.title: Derivation of the Four-Factor Formula for Infinite Multiplication Factor
derivations.conditions: Infinite thermal reactor containing natural or enriched uranium fuel and a moderator.
steps: Consider N<sub>T</sub> thermal neutrons initiating fission in generation n. These neutrons produce N<sub>T</sub> η fast neutrons, where η is the number of fast neutrons produced per thermal neutron absorbed in fuel.
Due to fast fission of <sup>238</sup>U by unmoderated neutrons, the total number of fast neutrons becomes N<sub>T</sub> η ε, where ε is the fast fission factor (ε > 1).
These fast neutrons slow down through the resonance absorption region of <sup>238</sup>U. A fraction p, called the resonance escape probability, avoids capture and reaches thermal energies.
The number of thermalized neutrons is therefore N<sub>T</sub> η ε p.
Out of these thermalized neutrons, a fraction f (thermal utilization factor) is absorbed specifically by the fuel rather than the moderator, structural materials, or fission products.
The total number of thermal neutrons in generation (n+1) is N<sub>T+1</sub> = N<sub>T</sub> ε p f η.
By definition, the infinite multiplication factor k<sub>inf</sub> is N<sub>T+1} / N<sub>T</sub>.
derivations.result: k_inf = epsilon cdot p cdot f cdot eta

derivations.title: Condition for Criticality in a Finite Reactor
derivations.conditions: Homogeneous thermal reactor considering neutron leakage.
steps: The effective multiplication factor k<sub>eff</sub> accounts for both neutron production/absorption in an infinite medium and neutron leakage from the finite boundary.
Let L<sub>f</sub> be the probability that a fast neutron does not leak out during slowing down, and L<sub>t</sub> be the probability that a thermal neutron does not leak out before absorption.
Thus, k<sub>eff</sub> = k_{inf} cdot L_f cdot L_t.
Using Fermi age theory, the fast non-leakage probability is approximated as L_f = e^{-B^2 	au}, where B<sup>2</sup> is the buckling of the reactor and τ is the Fermi age.
Using one-group diffusion theory, the thermal non-leakage probability is approximated as L_t =  rac{1}{1 + B^2 L_t^2}, where L<sub>t</sub> is the thermal diffusion length.
Combining these yields the critical equation: k_{inf} = (1 + B^2 	au)(1 + B^2 L_t^2) e^{B^2 	au} (or simplified as k_{inf} / (1 + B^2 M^2) = 1 where M is the migration length).

formula_sheet.name: Infinite Multiplication Factor
formula_sheet.equation_html: k_{inf} = epsilon cdot p cdot f cdot eta
formula_sheet.variables: ε = fast fission factor, p = resonance escape probability, f = thermal utilization factor, η = reproduction factor
formula_sheet.conditions: Infinite reactor geometry with no neutron leakage

formula_sheet.name: Effective Multiplication Factor
formula_sheet.equation_html: k_{eff} = k_{inf} cdot L_f cdot L_t
formula_sheet.variables: L<sub>f</sub> = fast non-leakage probability, L<sub>t</sub> = thermal non-leakage probability

graphs_and_experiments.title: Neutron Flux Distribution in a Finite Reactor
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bell-shaped cosine curve representing thermal neutron flux φ(r) plotted against spatial coordinate r from center to edge of a cylindrical or spherical reactor.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Neutron flux is maximum at the center of the reactor core and drops smoothly to zero at (or slightly beyond, due to extrapolation distance) the extrapolated boundary.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in TGT/PGT to identify where fission rate and power density are maximal within a reactor core.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Fermi Age Moderation Spectrum
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A Gaussian or lethargy distribution curve showing the slowing down density q(r, τ) of neutrons as a function of spatial displacement or age τ.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how fast fission neutrons spread out spatially as they lose energy through elastic collisions before reaching thermal energy.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in PGT numericals and theoretical questions regarding slowing down length and Fermi age theory.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Reactor Startup and Reactivity Insertion Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Graph of neutron density (or power level on a log scale) versus time following a step increase in reactivity (ρ > 0).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows an initial jump due to prompt neutrons followed by an exponential rise governed by the delayed neutron precursors (reactor period T).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Evaluates understanding of reactor kinetics and the critical role of delayed neutrons in safe operation.

solved_numericals.question: In a thermal nuclear reactor, if the reproduction factor η is 1.33, the thermal utilization factor f is 0.85, the resonance escape probability p is 0.90, and the fast fission factor ε is 1.03, calculate the infinite multiplication factor (k_inf).
solution_steps: Write down the formula for the infinite multiplication factor: k_{inf} = epsilon cdot p cdot f cdot eta
Substitute the given values: ε = 1.03, p = 0.90, f = 0.85, η = 1.33
Calculate the product: k_{inf} = 1.03 	imes 0.90 	imes 0.85 	imes 1.33
Compute final numerical value: k_{inf} approx 1.045

solved_numericals.question: A large thermal reactor has an infinite multiplication factor k_{inf} = 1.08. The thermal diffusion length L_t is 5 cm and the Fermi age τ is 35 cm<sup>2</sup>. Assuming critical condition (k_{eff} = 1) and using one-group diffusion theory with L_f ≈ 1 - B<sup>2</sup>τ, find the geometric buckling B<sup>2</sup>.
solution_steps: Write the critical equation relation: k_{eff} =  rac{k_{inf}}{(1 + B^2 L_t^2)(1 + B^2 	au)} = 1
Rearrange to get: (1 + B^2 L_t^2)(1 + B^2 	au) = k_{inf}
Expand the binomial product, neglecting higher-order terms in B<sup>2</sup> if B<sup>2</sup> is small: 1 + B^2(L_t^2 + 	au) = k_{inf}

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the reactivity ρ of a reactor whose effective multiplication factor k_{eff} is 1.05. Express your answer in dimensionless units and in percent.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for reactivity: ho =  rac{k_{eff} - 1}{k_{eff}}
Divide by k_{eff}: ho =  rac{0.05}{1.05} approx 0.0476

assumptions_and_limitations: One-group diffusion theory assumes all neutrons are monoenergetic at thermal energy, neglecting the thermal Maxwellian energy spectrum.
Fermi age theory assumes slowing down occurs by continuous moderation (continuous slowing down approximation), which is inaccurate for hydrogen where energy loss per collision is large.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Prompt neutrons alone determine the steady-state control time scale of a nuclear reactor.
common_misconceptions.correct: Delayed neutrons dictate the effective reactor period and make safe mechanical control possible.
common_misconceptions.why: Prompt neutron generation time is on the order of microseconds, making manual or mechanical feedback far too slow without delayed neutrons.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A reactor with k_{inf} > 1 is always critical regardless of its physical dimensions.
common_misconceptions.correct: A reactor must exceed its critical size so that neutron production overcomes leakage (k_{eff} = 1).
common_misconceptions.why: If a reactor is too small, high neutron leakage causes k_{eff} to drop below 1 even if k_{inf} > 1.

quick_revision: Fission of <sup>235</sup>U produces ~2.5 neutrons per absorption and releases ~200 MeV energy.
Four-factor formula: k_{inf} = epsilon p f eta.
Criticality condition: k_{eff} = 1; Subcritical: k_{eff} < 1; Supercritical: k_{eff} > 1.
Good moderators have high scattering cross-section, low absorption cross-section, and large ξ.
Migration length squared equals thermal diffusion length squared plus Fermi age: M<sup>2</sup> = L_t^2 + 	au.
